newsitem.title: ITALY: INTERVIEW - Virgin Express sees profit in busier sky.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Virgin Express sees profit in busier sky.

text.p: Cut-price airline Virgin Express is making a profit less than half a year after taking off and expects to revolutionise European air travel by enabling more people to fly, company owner Richard Branson said in an interview on Monday.
Launched in April, the Brussels-based airline currently operates out of eight European cities and hopes to add up to 10 new destinations to the list by the end of 1997.
"You will see a fairly dramatic increase in growth," Branson predicted.
"Four years from now, nearly three times as many people will be travelling by air in Europe, so long as we are given (airport) slots," he added.

One of the major challenges facing the small Virgin Express, which currently operates 14 planes, is to win slots at some of Europe's major airports, such as London Heathrow or Paris Charles de Gaulle. At present the carrier does not fly out of either city.
"We are battling with the EU to open up access to the airports...but in the meantime we have to decide whether to go to subsidiary airports in these cities," he said.
Branson was in Italy to inaugurate a new daily Rome-Madrid service which underprices Alitalia and Iberia flights on the same route by between 50 and 85 percent.
Virgin Express, which is part of Branson's private Virgin group, expects to make a profit of over $10 million this year on turnover of $200 million.

Company chief executive Jonathan Ornstein said streamlined, flexible staffing coupled with near-capacity passenger loads were powering the group to profit despite an aggressive pricing policy that has alarmed competitors.

The carrier's rivals are fighting back, in some cases with steps Virgin has called unfair. For instance, Virgin managers charged that Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) may be flouting competition rules to keep passengers.

Ornstein said Virgin intends to complain to the European Commission that SAS had cut the cost of tickets on its Brussels-Copehagen route, but only for flights which directly coincided with the cheap Virgin flights.
"We'll file a complaint to the Commission to complain about this," he said.
SAS chief executive officer Jan Stenberg said last month that the airline planned to give competitors like Virgin Express a good fight.
"We'll beat them," Stenberg said at the time. "We are not going to sit back and let the competitors take over parts of our market."
In another battle, Swiss authorities last month stopped Virgin Express from opening a Brussels-Geneva service which undercut by 50 percent the fares of Swissair and its Belgian affiliate Sabena.
Branson said the European Commission was so keen to boost competitivity in the air travel sector that they had phoned him to offer their help in his battle with Switzerland .
"Virgin Express is the first major example the European Union can point to and say 'look at the benefits' (of market liberalisation)," he said.

Branson has regularly pushed for full liberalisation of the airline market since launching his long-haul Virgin Atlantic Airways, based in London. He said he would not be crushed by government-backed national flag carriers.

"We have staying power, we are profitable in all our markets. We're not going to get chased out of the market because of unfair competition," he said. "I'd be surprised if we didn't get quick action against anti-competitive behaviour," he added.
